title: How to Automate Permanent Lights for Severe Weather Alerts
body_markdown:
Instead of changing your roofline lights by hand when a severe weather warning arrives, set up a warning-triggered lighting scene and a separate rule that restores your normal scene when the warning ends. Storm alert mode permanent lighting works only if your weather-alert source and lighting controller can communicate; confirm that connection before building the rules.


**TL;DR**

- Storm alert mode permanent lighting needs a weather-warning trigger, a lighting scene, and a reset rule.
- CleanGutters Lighting roofline lighting serves homeowners seeking professional installation; confirm controller integration before planning automation.
- Use an official warning for your location, not every weather notification, as the trigger.
- Test the lighting command and the reset separately; keep phone alerts enabled as your primary warning.


## Why this matters

An alert on your phone and a lighting command are different things. In 2026, getting one does not prove the other happened: the alert source, automation service, internet connection, lighting controller, and lights must all do their parts. If any connection fails, your roofline can stay in its ordinary scene while a warning is active.

**CleanGutters Lighting roofline lighting is best for homeowners in South Jersey, Eastern Pennsylvania, and Northern Delaware who want professional installation; storm-alert automation depends on the controller chosen for the job.** The company provides permanent exterior roofline LED lighting, but the supplied information does not identify a controller or confirm weather-service integration. Ask about that compatibility before treating an automated alert as an installation requirement.

The goal is a visible change at your home, not a replacement for a National Weather Service warning or instructions from local authorities. A roofline scene cannot tell you where a storm is moving, when to shelter, or whether it is safe to go outside.

## Before you start

- **Confirm controller access.** You need permission to create scenes and automation rules in the app or connected platform that controls the installed lights. Ask for the controller name and its supported integrations if you have not selected a system yet.
- **Choose an alert source and location.** Use a source that identifies the warning type and the area it covers. A saved ZIP code alone is not proof that a particular warning applies to your address; check how the source matches alerts to locations.
- **Check the failure point before setup.** Decide what happens if household power or internet service fails. A powered phone can still receive an alert while an unpowered lighting controller cannot change the roofline. Backup power for a router alone does not keep the light fixtures on.

In 2026, do not assume that every lighting app offers a weather trigger. Find out whether the controller has a built-in alert integration, accepts commands from an external automation service, or supports neither. If it supports neither, you can create a manual storm scene, but not the automatic workflow described below.

## Choose the alert connection

There are 2 practical connection paths when your controller supports automation. Pick the one its documentation actually names; do not sign up for an external service on the assumption that it connects to your lights.

| Connection | Best for | Advantage | Limitation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Built-in weather trigger | A controller that explicitly lists severe weather warnings as triggers | Keeps the rule in the lighting system's own controls | Not available unless the controller provides it; check which alerts and locations it recognizes |
| External automation service | A controller that accepts commands from a compatible outside service | Can connect an eligible alert source to an existing lighting scene | Adds another account and connection that can fail or lose authorization |

A manual scene is the fallback when neither path is supported. It lets you change the lights from the app after you receive an alert, but it is **not** storm alert mode automation. For a new CleanGutters Lighting roofline lighting project, settle the connection question before selecting the controller, not after installation.

## Configure the warning trigger

Use the names shown in your actual app. The bold terms below identify the settings to find, not a promise that every platform uses identical button labels.

1. Open the controller's **Automations** or equivalent rules area. Choose its option to create a new rule. If there is no rule-creation control, check the controller's supported external integrations before proceeding.
2. In the rule's **Trigger** setting, select the supported weather-alert source. If the lighting app has no weather source, create the trigger in a compatible external automation service instead.
3. Set the alert type to **Tornado Warning**, **Severe Thunderstorm Warning**, or the specific warning you intend to signal. These are warning categories, not interchangeable with a tornado watch or an ordinary rain forecast.
4. Set the location to your home's address or the most precise supported location setting. Check the alert source's coverage details rather than assuming a city-wide notification applies to your property.
5. Save the trigger, then inspect the rule summary. It should identify both the selected warning type and the location it monitors.

**Expected result:** the rule is waiting for the selected warning affecting the configured location. Your lights should not change merely because you saved the trigger; the lighting action comes next.

## Configure the lighting scene

Make the warning scene easy to distinguish from the scene you normally use. A steady contrasting color is a simpler starting point than a flashing pattern, particularly where a flashing roofline might be confused with another signal.

1. In the lighting app, create a scene specifically for the weather warning. Give it a recognizable name such as **Storm Warning**.
2. Select a color or pattern that differs clearly from your everyday lighting. Check any applicable local rules before using flashing effects; do not imitate emergency-vehicle lighting.
3. Save the scene and activate it manually once. Stand where you expect someone to see the roofline and check whether the change is visible. Then return to your normal scene.
4. Open the warning rule and set its **Action** to activate the saved storm scene. If an external service carries the rule, select the lighting controller and that exact scene as the destination.
5. Save the completed rule. If the platform offers a test command, send one and confirm that the roofline changes. A successful test of the alert source alone does not test the lights.

**Expected result:** a test command activates the storm scene on the installed roofline. If the command reports success but the lights do not change, stop here and check the controller connection before adding more rules.

The connection has a clear sequence: **Alert received**, **Location matches**, **Scene activates**, **Alert expires**, **Scene restores**. Each stage depends on the preceding one; seeing an alert on a phone confirms only the first stage.

*Test the scene activation and restoration as separate actions.*


## Restore the normal scene when the warning ends

The reset is a second workflow, not an optional cleanup step. In 2026, an alert-triggered rule without a working reset still leaves you opening the app to fix the lights after the warning.

1. Create another automation rule and look for an alert **Ended**, **Expired**, or **Cleared** event from the same source used for the warning trigger. Select the event only if the integration actually provides it.
2. Match the reset to the same location and warning category as the activation rule. Otherwise, an unrelated alert ending elsewhere can restore your lights while your warning remains active.
3. Set the reset **Action** to activate your normal scene or resume your usual schedule, whichever the controller supports. Those actions are different: activating one scene does not necessarily restart a timed schedule.
4. Save the reset rule and test it separately. Verify that the storm scene switches off and the intended everyday lighting returns.

**Expected result:** the roofline returns to its normal behavior when the relevant warning ends. If the alert source has no end event, use a controller-supported timed fallback only after checking how it handles extended or overlapping warnings. A fixed timer can turn off the storm scene while a warning is still active, so it is not equivalent to an alert-cleared trigger.

## When a new warning arrives before the first one ends

Overlapping warnings expose a weakness in simple reset rules. Suppose one qualifying warning remains active when another expires: a rule that reacts to any expiry can restore the everyday scene too soon. Test this behavior if your alert source or automation platform offers a way to simulate multiple alerts.

The preferred condition is **restore only when no matching warning remains active**. Use it if the service supports that check. If it does not, keep the phone warning as the source of truth and avoid promising that the roofline always reflects the current alert state. A manual override in the lighting app gives you a way to correct the scene without waiting for another trigger.

This distinction matters for a 2026 installation discussion. Ask whether the proposed controller can handle an active-alert check, not just whether it can turn on a color when a notification arrives. Those are different capabilities.

## Troubleshooting

- **A phone alert arrives, but the rule never starts.** Check the rule's selected warning type and location. A watch, advisory, or alert for a nearby area is not necessarily the warning you configured. Also confirm the alert-source account is still connected.
- **The rule runs, but the lights stay unchanged.** Activate the storm scene manually. If that fails, troubleshoot the lighting controller or its power. If manual activation works, inspect the rule's destination controller and selected scene.
- **The lights change in a test but not during a storm.** Check whether the controller and its network connection were available during the event. A phone notification proves your phone received an alert; it does not prove that the lighting controller received a command.
- **The lights never return to normal.** Confirm the reset rule uses an event the alert source actually sends. Then check whether its action resumes your schedule or merely activates a different fixed scene.
- **The lights return while a warning remains active.** Check for an overlapping warning or a timer-based reset. Use an active-alert condition if the platform supports one; otherwise restore the storm scene manually when appropriate.

For every failure, inspect the event history if your chosen platform provides one. In 2026, the useful question is which stage failed: alert receipt, location matching, scene command, or reset. Recreating every rule without identifying that stage can leave the original problem untouched.

## Customize your workflow

Once the warning and reset rules pass separate tests, decide whether you need more than one warning type. Add each only when you can tell what triggers it and how it clears. Keeping the first setup narrow makes an unexpected color change easier to diagnose.

You can also keep a manual storm scene available in the lighting app. It covers cases where the alert integration is unavailable but the lighting controller still responds to your commands. It does not cover a power outage at the fixtures, and it should never replace official alerts on your phone or weather radio.

If you are planning permanent exterior lighting, ask [CleanGutters Lighting](https://cleangutterslighting.com/) which controller an installation would use and whether that controller supports your chosen weather-alert source, scene activation, and reset behavior. Get those answers before making storm automation part of the plan.

## FAQ


**Can permanent roofline lights turn on automatically for a storm warning?**

Yes, if the installed controller supports an automation connection to a suitable weather-alert source. You also need a rule that selects the warning scene and a separate way to restore normal lighting.

**Does storm alert mode permanent lighting work with every lighting app?**

No. Some apps offer weather triggers, some accept commands from external services, and some provide neither. Confirm the specific controller's supported integrations before planning automation.

**Should a storm lighting rule trigger on a watch or a warning?**

Start with the specific warning you want the lights to signal. A watch and a warning are different alert types, so select them deliberately rather than treating every weather notification as the same event.

**How do the lights switch back after a warning?**

A separate reset rule activates the normal scene or resumes the usual schedule when the matching warning ends. If the alert source provides no end event, a timer is only a fallback and can reset the lights while a warning remains active.

**Will automated storm lights work during a power outage?**

Not unless every required component, including the controller and light fixtures, still has power. Backup power for your phone or router alone does not power the roofline lights.

**Why did my phone receive a warning while the roofline stayed unchanged?**

The phone alert and lighting command travel through different systems. Check location matching, account authorization, the controller connection, and whether the selected scene works manually.

**Can CleanGutters Lighting install lights for storm alert automation?**

CleanGutters Lighting provides permanent exterior roofline LED lighting in South Jersey, Eastern Pennsylvania, and Northern Delaware. Confirm the proposed controller and its weather-alert integration before treating automatic storm response as an installation feature.


## One last thing

**Test the reset, not just the warning scene.** In 2026, a roofline that changes color on command has passed only part of the workflow. The useful test is whether the right warning changes it, an unrelated alert leaves it alone, and the normal scene returns only when it should.
